summary: William Robertson worked in history and archaeology after studying divinity at the University of Edinburgh (1733–1741). He later served as the university's Principal from 1762 to 1792 and was a member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh.

William Ross Hardie studied at the University of Edinburgh (~1876–1880) and Balliol College, Oxford (~1880–1884). He held posts at the University of Oxford (~1884–1895) and the University of Edinburgh (~1895–1916).

William Roxburgh was an Indologist who studied at the University of Edinburgh and Marischal College under John Hope and Alexander Monro. He served as Chief Botanist for the East India Company and led the Indian Botanic Garden (1793–1813).

William S. Waldron, active in Buddhist studies and philosophy, earned his PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison under Minoru Kiyota, Ichijo Ogawa, and Seiki Miyashita. He held posts at Otani University and Middlebury College (attested 2003).

William Sandys Wright Vaux was an Indologist and historian who studied at Balliol College, Oxford. He served as Keeper of Coins and Medals at the British Museum (1861–1870) and Secretary of the Royal Asiatic Society (1876–1885).
William Sax is a scholar of Indology and religious studies. He held posts at the University of Canterbury (attested 2000) and Heidelberg University, where he became Professor Emeritus in 2025.

William Sidney Allen worked in linguistics and Indology, earning his PhD at Cambridge under Arthur James Beattie and Harold Walter Bailey. He lectured at SOAS (1948–1951) and was Professor of Comparative Philology at Cambridge (1955–1982).
William Spottiswoode, working in Indology and other fields, studied at Balliol College, Oxford (1842–1845). He held posts at Balliol College and Eyre & Spottiswoode in 1846.

William Stede worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics, earning his PhD from Leipzig (~1908–1913). He taught at Liverpool and SOAS, was affiliated with the University of London, and served as President of the Pali Text Society (1950–1958).
William Taylor worked in Indology. He served as a missionary with the London Missionary Society (1824–1845) and was a cataloguer at Madras College.

William Van Gordon, active in Buddhist and religious studies, founded the Awake to Wisdom Centre for Meditation and Mindfulness Research. He held a post as a research psychologist at Nottingham Trent University (attested 2015).

William Ward worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at Brearley Theological Academy and under John Fawcett at Ewood Hall Academy (1797), served at the Serampore Mission (~1799–1823), and founded Serampore College in 1818.

William Wilfred Webb worked in Indology and history/archaeology after studying at the University of Aberdeen (~1880–1884). He served as Surgeon-Captain in the Bengal Army (~1884–1894) and Secretary of the Army Medical School (1893–1902).

William Wilson Hunter worked in Indology and history, studying at Glasgow, Paris, and Bonn. He served in the Indian Civil Service (~1862–1887), as Vice-Chancellor of Calcutta University (1886–1887), and as Vice-President of the Royal Asiatic Society (~1895–1900).

William Woodville Rockhill was a scholar of Tibetology, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at the École spéciale militaire de Saint-Cyr (~1871–1873) and with Léon Feer and Philippe Édouard Foucaux (~1876–1880).

Linguist William Wright studied at St Andrews, Halle-Wittenberg, and Leiden. He taught Arabic at University College London and Trinity College Dublin before working at the British Museum (1861–1870) and as Adams Professor of Arabic at Cambridge (1870–1889).
William Yates worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Bristol Baptist College (1812), under William Carey (~1815–1834), and later earned degrees from Brown University in 1831 and 1839.

Indologist Willibald Kirfel studied and habilitated at the University of Bonn under Hermann Jacobi. He worked as a librarian at Bonn University Library and served as ordinary Professor of Indology at Bonn from 1922 to 1953.

Willy Bang-Kaup studied at KU Leuven under Charles-Joseph de Harlez de Deulin and taught Germanistics there (1895–1914). In Iranian/Central Asian linguistics, he later held professorships in Turkish linguistics at Frankfurt (1917) and Berlin (1918).

Willy Baruch worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Sinology, studying under Heinrich Lüders, Friedrich Weller, and Willibald Kirfel before completing his PhD at Bonn. He taught Manchu at the Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales (1933–1935).
